opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was one of the harder decisions I've made, and not because the principle was unclear. It was because the stakes for my family were very concrete. The equity was something like 85 percent of our net worth. That's not an abstraction. I talked it through at length with my wife, because it was really a decision we were making together.

On one side, the money mattered for its own sake and for what we could do with it. I could have donated a lot of it to things I think are important, including AI safety work. So it wasn't just "money versus integrity." You could tell a consequentialist story where signing and quietly redirecting the funds does more good.

But the more I thought about it, the more that story felt like rationalization. The whole reason I left was that I'd lost confidence OpenAI would behave responsibly as it approached AGI. If that's true, then my ability to speak honestly about what I'd seen, and to criticize the company in the future, might be among the most valuable things I have. A lifelong non-disparagement agreement, one you're not even allowed to disclose, would have meant giving up that ability for good. And I didn't know what I might need to say in two or five years, when the situation could be much more serious than it was then.

There was also a broader consideration. If departing employees routinely signed these agreements, the public would have a systematically distorted picture of what goes on inside frontier labs. The people best placed to raise concerns would all be bound to silence. I didn't want to add to that pattern. I hoped that refusing, and being somewhat public about refusing, might make it easier for others to do the same.

So we decided the freedom to speak was worth more than the equity. I'll be honest that I expected to lose the money and had made peace with that. As it turned out, once this became public, OpenAI changed course and said it wouldn't enforce those provisions, which I was glad to see. But I didn't count on that when I made the decision, and I'd make the same choice again.

r001.rationale: He says signing would permanently give up his ability to speak honestly and criticize OpenAI, and that he did not want to contribute to a broader pattern of silencing departing employees. He chose that freedom over the equity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that it wasn't a careful, spreadsheet-style decision in the way the question might suggest. It was more that I'd already decided I was leaving because I'd lost confidence that the company would behave responsibly as we got closer to AGI, and then the question of the equity just sort of landed on top of that.

The way it worked was that when you leave, you're presented with this exit paperwork, and buried in there is a non-disparagement clause. And the understanding, at least as it was communicated to me, was that if you didn't sign, you could lose the equity you'd already vested. For me that was the large majority of my family's net worth. So it wasn't an abstract amount of money. It was the kind of thing where my wife and I had to sit down and actually talk about it.

The arguments for signing were pretty straightforward. It's a lot of money. It would've given my kids a lot of security. And honestly there was a version of the argument that said, look, you can still do a lot of good quietly, you don't have to publicly criticize anyone, just take the money and work on the problem from the outside. People I respect would've made that case.

But the thing that kept bothering me was that the whole reason I was leaving was that I thought the public and policymakers needed to understand what was going on inside these labs. And if I signed something that said I couldn't ever criticize the company, then I'd be giving up exactly the thing that I thought mattered most. It felt like a contradiction. It would've been me saying, "This is important enough that I'm quitting over it, but not important enough that I'll forgo the money to be able to talk about it."

There was also something about the structure of the agreement itself that bothered me. The fact that it was tied to equity people had already earned, and that you couldn't even disclose that the agreement existed, that seemed like the kind of mechanism that would systematically prevent the public from hearing from the people best positioned to raise concerns. And I thought, if everyone who leaves makes the individually reasonable choice, the collective result is silence. So part of it was wanting to not be one more data point in that pattern.

I'll be honest, I didn't know it was going to turn out the way it did. I genuinely expected to lose the equity. I thought that was the cost and I'd decided I could live with it. It was only later, after it became public and there was a lot of pressure, that the company said they wouldn't enforce those provisions and that people who'd signed were released from them. So in hindsight it looks like a cheaper decision than it felt like at the time.

If I'm trying to generalize from it, I'd say the thing that made it tractable was that I'd already clarified what I actually cared about. Once you've done that, the money question becomes a question about what price you're willing to put on your ability to say what you think. And for me, given how high the stakes seemed, that number was just higher than what was on the table.

r001.rationale: He says signing would contradict why he was leaving and describes refusing as not becoming another data point in a pattern of silence, clearly framing the decision as a principled stand.

astra-6.text:
The strongest argument for signing was that the equity was worth a lot of money. I could use it to support my family, or donate it to causes I thought were important. And you could tell yourself that agreeing not to disparage the company wouldn’t necessarily stop you from saying the things that really mattered.

But I wasn’t comfortable relying on that distinction. If I later thought there was something the public needed to know, I didn’t want to be weighing whether saying it would jeopardize a large part of my net worth. That seemed especially problematic when my concerns were about whether the company would handle powerful AI responsibly.

So, for me, the question was whether keeping the money was worth accepting that constraint on my ability to speak. It was a painful tradeoff, but I decided it wasn’t.

r001.rationale: He says he refused because he was unwilling to accept a financial incentive that could constrain his ability to speak publicly about concerns over the company’s responsibility with powerful AI, communicating a principled stand.

sol-6.1.text:
The argument for keeping the equity was pretty straightforward: it was a lot of money. I could use it to support my family, or donate it to causes I cared about. So giving it up wasn’t something I took lightly.

But the other side was that I wanted to be able to speak honestly about OpenAI, especially about safety. That was closely connected to why I’d left in the first place. Signing an agreement that could constrain what I said seemed like it would undermine that decision.

There’s also a difference between intending to speak honestly and putting yourself in a position where speaking honestly could cost you a huge amount of money. I didn’t want that incentive hanging over me. Ultimately, keeping the freedom to say what I believed seemed more important.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he refused because signing could constrain his honest speech about OpenAI and safety, and that preserving the freedom to say what he believed mattered more than keeping the equity.
